title: How TCS keeps an AI test-fixing loop safe
caption:
A test fails in CI. Do you let an AI agent fix it?

TCS runs an agentic test orchestrator in production for banking and insurance clients, and the part I found most useful is how tightly it controls the self-repair loop.

What the loop does:
- Runs the generated test and classifies the failure
- Sends only code errors to a fixing agent
- Keeps connectivity and auth errors away from the fixer
- Rejects patches that are empty, add unexpected files or change file size wildly
- Stops retrying when the retry policy says so

TCS reports about 88% less effort on roughly 100 scenarios. That is their own internal benchmark, so treat it as a data point, not a promise.

Save this for when you design your own agent repair loop. Which check would you add first? Tell me in the comments.

Source: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/how-tcs-built-an-agentic-test-orchestrator-with-amazon-bedrock-agentcore/

slides.headline: Should an AI agent fix your ==failing tests?==
slides.sub: How TCS bounds the self-repair loop in its test orchestrator.

slides.title: The loop sits after generation
paragraphs: TCS's Agentic Test Orchestrator generates tests for banking and insurance clients, then an **execution agent** runs them.
That agent's job is a fixed workflow, written as a LangGraph state graph: fetch, execute, fix, save.
slides.callout: AgentCore Runtime hosts and isolates the agent.

slides.title: The execution workflow

steps.title: Fix
steps.text: Code errors only, if retries remain

slides.foot: A ==fixed step order== and a ==bounded retry loop==.

slides.title: Why an explicit graph
paragraphs: An explicit state graph gives a **fixed step order**, so the agent cannot wander.
The retry loop is **bounded** by a retry policy: when it says stop, the loop ends.
slides.callout: The model proposes fixes. The graph decides what happens next.

slides.title: Classify before you fix
slides.body: Not every failure deserves a code change.
slides.after: Connectivity and auth failures are ==**never sent to the code fixer.**==

slides.title: The fixer gets a small brief
paragraphs: The fixing agent receives a **constrained error context**, not the whole project.
It proposes a **targeted correction** for that one failure.

slides.title: Patch-shape checks
items: Reject extreme changes in file size
Anything rejected is not saved as a fix
slides.foot: Cheap checks that catch a runaway ==rewrite.==

slides.label: less effort on about 100 test scenarios
slides.context: About 200 hours manual versus about 24 hours with the orchestrator. TCS ran this as a controlled internal benchmark. Results vary by workload.
